title: How to Make a Cleaning Checklist You'll Actually Use
description: Most cleaning checklists get ignored. Here's how to make one that works for ADHD brains: short, visible, specific and satisfying to check off.
intro:
You print a beautiful cleaning checklist. You stick it on the fridge. You use it for three days. Then it becomes part of the fridge, like a magnet you stopped seeing years ago.

Sound familiar? It's not the idea of a checklist that fails. Checklists are actually great for our brains, because they hold the plan so we don't have to. It's usually the *design* of the checklist that doesn't fit how we work.

Here's how to make one (or pick one) that you'll keep using.

sections.heading: Why checklists help
sections.body:
Checklists take the thinking out of cleaning. Instead of deciding what to do next (which drains energy), you look at the list and do the next thing.

They also give you a little burst of satisfaction every time you check a box. That's a small reward our brains really respond to.

sections.heading: Rule 1: Short enough to finish
sections.body:
A checklist with 25 items feels impossible, so we don't start. Keep daily lists to five to seven items. Weekly lists can be a bit longer, but split them into short sections.

A list you finish feels great. A list you abandon halfway feels like failing, and nobody wants to come back to that.

sections.heading: Rule 2: Specific, not vague
sections.body:
"Clean the kitchen" is not a task. It's a project with a dozen hidden steps. Our brains stall on vague items.

Make each item a single, clear action:

- "Load the dishwasher"
- "Wipe the counters"
- "Take out the trash"

When you know exactly what "done" looks like, it's easy to start.

sections.heading: Rule 3: Put it where the work happens
sections.body:
A bathroom checklist should be in the bathroom (inside a cabinet door works great). A kitchen list goes in the kitchen. A launch pad list goes by the door.

If you have to go find the checklist, it won't get used. Put it right where your eyes are when the task needs doing.

sections.heading: Rule 4: Make it reusable
sections.body:
Slip your checklist into a sheet protector or a dry-erase pocket and use a dry-erase marker. Check things off, wipe it clean tomorrow.

No reprinting, no wasted paper and no excuse to skip because you ran out of copies.

sections.heading: Rule 5: Include a low-energy version
sections.body:
Give every checklist a "bare minimum" version for rough days. Mark two or three items with a little ★ symbol. On hard days, only do the marked ones.

This keeps the checklist from becoming something you avoid. It bends with you.

sections.heading: Rule 6: Refresh it every few months
sections.body: Our brains love novelty. After a while, even a good checklist can fade into the background. Every few months, change the color, the layout or the spot where it hangs. It sounds small, but it can wake the habit back up.

sections.heading: Rule 7: Celebrate the check
sections.body:
Don't skip the satisfying part. Use a bright marker, a sticker or a big fat checkmark. Some people love a "done" list on the back where they write what they finished, including things that weren't on the list.

It might feel a bit silly. But the checklist is only half about remembering. The other half is noticing that you did the thing, and our brains need that noticing more than most.

sections.heading: A sample daily checklist
sections.body:
Here's a simple one to start with:

- ☐ Dishes done or loaded ★
- ☐ Kitchen counters wiped
- ☐ Trash out if full ★
- ☐ 5-minute pick-up in the main room
- ☐ One load of laundry moved forward
- ☐ Launch pad cleared ★

Copy it onto a card, stick it where you'll see it and see how it goes this week.

outro:
Short, specific, visible and reusable. That's a checklist that works with our brains.
